description: We are students passionate about space technology, AI, and engineering. Our project, SYNORA, uses AI to monitor astronauts’ health and detect unusual changes during space missions. We are looking for motivated teammates interested in AI/ML, Python, electronics, and software development who are eager to innovate and work together.
summary:
AstroNot: space tools for researchers and curious minds

Astronomy tools are scattered across many websites, take time to learn, and often require downloading huge data files, which wastes researchers' time and turns beginners away. AstroNot brings them together on one website that runs entirely in the browser, with nothing to install.

Researchers get 13 tools for working with real data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. They can search observations, inspect FITS images, watch a patch of sky change over time, detect sources, compare images, build mosaics and measure spectra. AstroNot connects directly to IRSA's public SPHEREx archive: 208 TB in over 3 million files. Instead of downloading 72 MB files, it reads only the pixels each task needs, about 1 MB, straight from the archive. Heavy calculations run in Rust compiled to WebAssembly. Our spectra match the results of NASA/IPAC's official tool and arrive about six times faster.

For everyone else, six interactive experiences make it easy to find constellations, follow the Moon's phases, compare planets, mix nebula colours, plan meteor watching and learn galaxy shapes.

AstroNot is available in six languages, keeps users' files on their own devices, and uses real observations throughout.
details:
AstroNot is a browser-based platform that brings astronomy data analysis and space exploration into one place. It has two parts. For researchers, 13 scientific tools work on real NASA SPHEREx data from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): Observation Search, Sky Explorer, Time Machine, FITS Viewer, Image Differencing, Mosaic Builder, Spectrum Lab, Spectrophotometry, Forced Spectrophotometry, Source Detection, Catalog Cross-Match (Gaia DR3 and AllWISE), Light Curve Analysis and Motion Detector. For everyone else, six interactive experiences cover constellations, Moon phases, planet sizes, nebula colors, meteor showers and galaxy shapes.

Every tool follows the same workflow: choose a tool, open the bundled example or your own file, and explore the results. All computation happens on the user's device. Files are read locally and are never uploaded. Instead of downloading whole SPHEREx frames (about 70 MB each), the tools use HTTP Range requests to read only the bytes they need from IRSA's public S3 bucket, about 1 MB per frame.

BENEFITS

- No installation, no account and no setup. A link and a browser are enough.

- Privacy by design: there is no database, and user data stays on the device.

- Real NASA data instead of simulated examples.

- Trustworthy results: the tools are validated against Astropy, reproject, photutils and IRSA's own outputs. For example, Forced Spectrophotometry reproduced IRSA's method on all 352 exposures of the star BD+17 4708.

- Six languages: English, Azerbaijani, Turkish, Russian, Simplified Chinese and Spanish.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want to shorten the path from question to result. Researchers can check observations, measure spectra or compare epochs in minutes, without setting up a software environment. Students, teachers and curious people get a friendly entry point into the same real data that scientists use. Because the platform is free and runs on any modern browser, it also lowers the barrier for people in regions with limited access to computing resources.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no bundler, so any static host can serve the site.

- Rust compiled to WebAssembly for demanding calculations: FITS decoding, reprojection, source detection, catalog matching and CSV parsing. Every kernel has a JavaScript fallback.

- Cloudflare Pages for hosting, with one small Pages Function that forwards IRSA search requests, because the IRSA service does not send CORS headers.

- The Node.js test suite has more than 400 tests. Python with Astropy, reproject and SciPy provides reference comparisons.

- Data sources: NASA IRSA (SPHEREx), the Yale Bright Star Catalogue via NASA HEASARC, NASA SVS, NASA JPL, Gaia DR3 and AllWISE.

- Hardware: none beyond an ordinary computer or phone with a web browser.

CREATIVITY

AstroNot puts professional-grade science tools and playful learning experiences on the same platform, built on the same real data. Instead of building a heavy server, we moved the science into the browser with Rust and WebAssembly and read archive files partially over the network. This makes large-data astronomy feel instant and keeps it private. The tools can also pass data to each other, so a search result can go straight into a viewer or a measurement tool.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: when a tool cannot produce a reliable result, it says why. Results are never presented as official archive products, and known limits are documented.

- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, data tables alongside every plot, and reduced-motion support.

- Performance with large files: partial reads, WebAssembly kernels, and a Web Worker engine for gigabyte-scale images (in progress).

- Simplicity and sustainability: no build step, no database and minimal server code, so the project is easy to host and maintain.

- Proper credit for every dataset, image and font we used.
